title: Westminster Churches
subtitle: Circular trail · 7 churches · 2.3–3.3 km walk · about 100 minutes
transport: Westminster and St James's Park Underground stations are both close to the trail.
finish: You've visited all seven churches in the shadow of Parliament

stops.name: St Margaret's Church
stops.getThere: Walk up Lord North Street and along Great Peter Street to Millbank, then north along Abingdon Street past the Houses of Parliament.
stops.find: St Margaret's is the small church beside Westminster Abbey, facing Parliament Square. Go inside (it's free, Monday to Friday, 10.30am to 3.30pm) and look at the great stained-glass window behind the altar.

photo.caption: St Margaret's, with Big Ben behind

stops.question: The window shows the Crucifixion, with a royal couple kneeling in prayer below. The young woman later became Henry VIII's first wife. Who was she?
stops.hint: A Spanish princess, the first of Henry VIII's six wives.
stops.fact: Flemish glaziers made the window in the early 1500s to celebrate Catherine's betrothal. It passed through several owners before the parish bought it in 1758 for 400 guineas. St Margaret's has been the parish church of the House of Commons since 1614, and Winston Churchill married Clementine Hozier here in 1908.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, West Door
stops.getThere: Walk along The Sanctuary, round the north-west corner of the Abbey, to its west front between the two towers.
stops.find: Look up above the Great West Door at the row of ten modern statues.
stops.question: The fifth statue from the left is an American civil rights leader. What was his surname?
stops.fact: The ten statues honour Christian martyrs of the 20th century from around the world, including Oscar Romero and Dietrich Bonhoeffer. They were unveiled on 9 July 1998.

stops.name: Methodist Central Hall
stops.getThere: Cross Broad Sanctuary to the great domed hall on the corner of Tothill Street.
stops.find: Look for a plaque about a famous first meeting held here in 1946.
stops.question: Which organisation held the first meeting of its General Assembly here?
stops.hint: Its headquarters is now in New York.
stops.fact: The first UN General Assembly met here from 10 January to 14 February 1946. The hall is still a working Methodist church as well as a conference centre.

stops.name: The Guards' Chapel
stops.getThere: Walk west along Tothill Street, turn right through Queen Anne's Gate, then left along Birdcage Walk with St James's Park on your right, to Wellington Barracks.
stops.find: Find the Guards' Chapel, with a statue in front of it, and look closely at the old railings.

photo.caption: Find this statue outside the chapel

stops.question: The railings carry the royal cypher W IV R, left from the 1838 chapel. What was the king's name?
stops.hint: The sailor king, uncle of Queen Victoria.
stops.fact: On 18 June 1944 a V-1 flying bomb hit the chapel during the Sunday morning service, killing 121 people. Only the apse survived, with its candles still burning. Today's chapel was built in 1963.

stops.name: Westminster Cathedral
stops.getThere: Continue along Birdcage Walk, turn left into Buckingham Gate, then follow Stafford Place and Palace Street into Cathedral Walk, which leads to Victoria Street.
stops.find: Find the piazza in front of the striped cathedral with its tall bell tower.
stops.question: The red brick is banded with stripes of a pale stone named after a place in Dorset. Which stone?
stops.hint: It's also the name of a city in Oregon.
stops.fact: This is England's largest Catholic church. John Francis Bentley designed it in a Byzantine style, and it was built from 1895 to 1903. The bell tower is 284 feet (87 m) tall.

stops.name: St Matthew's Church
stops.getThere: Walk east along Victoria Street and turn right into Old Pye Street. St Matthew's is the grey stone church between Old Pye Street and Great Peter Street, with its parish school beside it.
stops.find: Go in through the base of the church's short, sturdy tower on Great Peter Street (the doors are open every day). Near the high altar, the church keeps a relic of its patron saint, St Matthew.
stops.question: Before Jesus called him to be a disciple, St Matthew had a job that made him very unpopular. What was it?
stops.hint: He collected money from his own people on behalf of the Romans.
stops.fact: Matthew was a tax collector in Capernaum, and the first Gospel in the Bible carries his name. George Gilbert Scott designed this church in 1849–51. Its tower was meant to carry a tall spire that was never built, so its base became the entrance. Fire almost destroyed the church in 1977, and it was rebuilt smaller and dedicated in 1984, keeping Ninian Comper's Lady Chapel.

stops.name: Smith Square Hall
stops.getThere: Continue east along Great Peter Street towards Parliament, then turn right into Lord North Street, which leads into Smith Square.
stops.find: The building in the middle of the square has a tower at each of its four corners.
stops.question: Legend says Queen Anne showed the architect what she wanted by kicking over a piece of furniture. What was it?
stops.fact: Thomas Archer built it as St John's church between 1713 and 1728. Bombed out in the Blitz, it reopened as a concert hall in 1969 and was renamed Smith Square Hall in 2024.
